title: Savitri walks after Yama
hook: Savitri meets fate with effort, and a book on desire argues the same.
carry: fate is real, and effort is still the means
tomorrow: a king borrows his son's youth. was it worth it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kichaka turned the order upside down: in a clash, dharma, then artha, then kama. Today, a woman told her husband's fate in advance, and what she did with it.

In the Mahabharata, Princess Savitri chooses her own husband: Satyavan, son of a blind king living in exile in the forest. Then the sage Narada brings terrible news. Satyavan has one year to live. Her father begs her to choose again. She won't. She marries him and counts the days. Three days before the end she fasts. On the last day she follows Satyavan into the forest, and when Yama, lord of death, comes for his life, she walks after Yama. She speaks with him so wisely that he grants her wish after wish, until one wish can only come true if Satyavan lives. Yama gives him back.
screen: `ONE YEAR TO LIVE.` → `SHE CHOOSES HIM ANYWAY.` → `SHE WALKS AFTER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Hindu thought has names for that struggle: daiva, fate, and purushakara, human effort. Savitri didn't deny the prophecy. She met it with everything she had: her vow, her fast, her feet on the road, her words. Many married Hindu women still honor her in the Vat Savitri fast, praying and tying threads around a banyan tree for their husbands' long lives. The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter takes up the same question with critics who say time and fate decide everything. Vatsyayana grants that luck is real. Then his answer: success depends on human effort as its means. Even what's bound to happen comes about through some means. And a person who does nothing enjoys no happiness. Ecclesiastes, in the Jewish and Christian Bibles, faces the same worry. In the King James Version it admits that "time and chance happeneth to them all," and later answers: "In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand." What they share: luck is real, and it isn't a reason to stop. And the honest difference. Ecclesiastes sets the not-knowing inside the work of God. Vatsyayana argues from means and effort, and his chapter doesn't turn to God to make the case.
screen: `DAIVA: FATE. PURUSHAKARA: EFFORT.` · `SAVITRI MET FATE WITH EFFORT.` · `EFFORT IS THE MEANS.` · `ECCLESIASTES: SOW ANYWAY.` · then, large: `A DESTINED SEED STILL NEEDS PLANTING.`

segments.voice: Say quietly, once, one small thing you'll do toward something whose outcome you can't control: an application, a hard conversation, a seed in a pot. If you pray, offer the effort and leave the outcome with God. If you don't, simply let it go. Then rest your hands open on your knees and breathe.
The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter: the answer to fate. Effort is the means, and a person who does nothing enjoys no happiness.
screen: `THE KAMA SUTRA'S ETHICS CHAPTER — today's word`.

segments.voice: For the road: fate is real, and effort is still the means. Savitri walked after Yama. See you tomorrow.
